speakeroldname: Hon. Roy MacLaren (Minister of State (Finance)) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-36, an Act to amend the Interest Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-36, an Act to amend the Interest Act, arises from February's Budget. Members may recall that the Budget outlined a number of proposals to improve the security of home owners. In fact, two Bills now before the House are in response to that initiative. Bill C-37, which we approved in principle yesterday, amends the National Housing Act to provide for the introduction of the Mortgage Rate Protection Program while Bill C-36 proposes amendments to the Interest Act.
One of the key elements in the Government's housing initiatives is these proposed amendments to the Interest Act. Those amendments will, first, strengthen the rights of mortgage borrowers by providing consumers with better disclosure of the terms of their mortgages. The amendments will also establish a statutory right for borrowers to prepay their mortgages with maximum penalties that strike a balance between the needs of both borrowers and lenders. Second, the amendments will increase the flexibility of the mortgage market. Third, they will provide a broader choice of mortgage instruments by permitting the development of new mortgage instruments.
Canadians have experienced a period of high and volatile mortgage rates. Conventional mortgage rates rose from just over 13 per cent in early 1980 to a peak approaching 22 per cent in the latter half of 1981. Since then, rates have returned to more traditional levels. In adapting to that unusual environment, available evidence suggests that the majority of borrowers renewed their mortgages for terms of less than two years or chose to take variable rate mortgages. We hope, however, that those experiences are now well behind us.
The steep decline in interest rates led many borrowers who had renewed their mortgages at high rates for longer terms to seek assistance from the Government in having their interest rates reduced. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Erola) have also received numerous complaints about the level of prepayment penalties that some lenders have demanded from consumers who wish to renegotiate or prepay existing high-

June 7, 1984
Interest Act
rate mortgages. Some lenders have shown an unwillingness to allow any prepayment.
The Government is sympathetic to the plight of those who have experienced difficulty in often trying circumstances. As Members know, the Government has demonstrated that it is prepared to take exceptional action in exceptional circumstances. It has introduced a number of measures to assist borrowers who are hardest hit and least able to cope. A joint government and industry task force was established to ensure the problems were identified as quickly as possible and dealt with in a flexible and responsive way. The co-operation of mortgage lenders in responding to problems in a flexible manner was essential and was forthcoming in most instances. Also the Canada Mortgage Renewal Plan has provided assistance to over 21,000 home owners.
The proposed amendments to the Interest Act now before us are one prong in the Government's efforts to improve home owner security. These proposals represent a comprehensive and balanced approach to this important problem and will minimize the risk of Canadians once again finding themselves in similar situations to those of recent years.
I should now like to discuss the proposed amendment contained in Bill C-36 in rather more detail. One comment that has been expressed on numerous occasions in letters and in other representations to the federal Government concerns the lack of information and understanding that borrowers had about the terms of the conditions of their mortgages. Bill C-36 proposes that mortgages be divided henceforth into two categories: first, mortgages over the prescribed amount of $150,000; second, mortgages equal to or less than $150,000. Mortgages in the second category, which encompass the vast majority of residential mortgages, will be subject to comprehensive disclosure requirements that will provide consumers with essential information on the terms and conditions of their mortgages, including prepayment rights and privileges. Lenders will have to fulfil these disclosure requirements when the mortgage is initiated and upon subsequent renewals. To permit "comparison shopping", lenders will be encouraged to disclose this information in advance.
The Interest Act requires that mortgage lenders disclose the rate of interest calculated yearly or half-yearly, not in advance. There is little disagreement among consumer groups, financial institutions and the public at large that most individuals do not understand this method of disclosing interest rates and cannot compare mortgage rates to other consumer loan rates. Lending institutions have suggested that the method of disclosing mortgage rates be modernized to reflect current lending techniques as practised in consumer and commercial lending. The lending institutions have suggested that mortgage rates be disclosed as an annual percentage, as is done in the United States.
The main reservations that have been expressed about adopting a new method of disclosing mortgage rates focus on the potential for a one-time disguised increase in mortgage
rates that could result from incorrect rounding of interest rates. In particular, while the Consumer's Association of Canada is generally supportive of modernizing the method of disclosing interest rates, concerns have been expressed about the rounding problem. As a result I suggest that the method of disclosing mortgage rates be examined at the committee stage of this Bill.
The proposed amendment in the Bill now before us attempts to balance the various facets of the mortgage market to ensure its continuing flexibility and responsiveness to the needs of borrowers and lenders. In this regard, the adoption of simple solutions could do more harm than good, making matters worse.
At various times there have been calls on the Government to set the prepayment penalty for all mortgages equal to three months' interest. While this proposal would allow borrowers to be relieved of their high mortgage obligations at relatively low cost, it remains a simplistic solution to a complex issue and can indeed do harm to the total mortgage market.
The adoption of this type of penalty in the majority of cases does not provide an appropriate balance of risks between lenders and borrowers, as it would interfere with the ability of financial institutions to match their assets and liabilities. Especially during periods of volatile interest rates, distortions in the mortgage market will occur. It is expected that all borrowers would find themselves more exposed to volatile interest rates and with fewer options available. This could both increase their costs and reduce their security by precluding the ability to lock in mortgage payments for reasonably long periods.
In recent years there has been considerable confusion in the minds of consumers about their prepayment privileges under the Interest Act. While the public's perception at times has been that a three-month interest prepayment penalty for longer-term mortgages is available on all mortgages, in reality mortgage contracts have a variety of prepayment penalties. Some contracts are silent on the subject and in those circumstances penalties are at the lender's discretion.
As I have already noted, some borrowers have complained about the level of proposed prepayment penalties and their ability to prepay the mortgage under any circumstances. The amendments contained in Bill C-36 propose that for mortgages of $150,000 or less borrowers have the right to prepay their mortgages upon the payment of the principal outstanding, any accrued interest and the prepayment charge. The method of calculating the maximum prepayment charge that a lender can impose is set out in the legislation. However, borrowers will not be prevented from negotiating more favourable prepayment conditions. It should be noted that the value of the prepayment charges will depend on a number of variables, including the outstanding principal, the amortization period, the decline in interest rates and the time remaining to the end of the term of the mortgage.
The basic principles underlying the proposed prepayment formula are that it should be a reasonable balance of the
June 7, 1984

interest of both parties and that it should not interfere with the vitality of the mortgage market. When mortgages are prepaid, lenders must relinquish their claims on existing mortgages and replace them with other mortgages. If current mortgage rates are lower than the contract rates, then lenders could experience losses. Accordingly the prepayment formula provides compensation to lenders for the losses incurred due to the prepayment and will thereby ensure a continuing supply of funds to the mortgage market. The proposed maximum for the prepayment penalty will be the present value of the difference, over the balance of the mortgage term, between the interest stream at the rate provided for in the mortgage being repaid and the currently prevailing market interest rate for mortgages of the same term. For partial prepayments, the charge shall be proportional to the amount of principal being prepaid.
In the event that interest rates remain unchanged or increase, there would be no prepayment charge. Due to the wide ranging debate and until recently the unspecified nature of the maximum prepayment penalty, some lenders have been inserting clauses into their mortgages and renewal agreements that require the borrower to waive his or her rights to future prepayment privileges. Bill C-36 proposes that borrowers cannot waive their statutory rights to disclosure or prepayment privileges.
Section 10 of the Interest Act provides borrowers with the right to prepay mortgages which have been in effect more than five years upon the payment of a penalty equal to three months' interest. The existence of Section 10 has contributed to the disappearance of long-term mortgages because lenders view it as an unequal distribution of risks between borrowers and lenders. There have been periodic requests for government action to encourage the development of a long-term mortgage market, and, accordingly, the Government is proposing initiatives to this end. As one step, Section 10 will be repealed to eliminate this legislative barrier to the development of very long-term mortgages and to make uniform the prepayment penalties for residential mortgages. The repeal of Section 10 would not apply retroactively to existing mortgages. No existing mortgage borrowers will be adversely affected by this change.
The repeal of Section 10, combined with the proposed present value prepayment penalty rules, is necessary if the longer-term mortgage market is to be revived. The new prepayment formula will help to ensure that mortgage funds are available to meet the market demand, while the repeal of Section 10 will remove an important barrier to longer-term mortgages.
The flexibility of the mortgage market can be improved by increasing the number of alternative mortgage instruments that are available to consumers. Variable rate mortgages have been available for a number of years and naturally gained in popularity during the recent period of high and volatile mortgage rates. While variable rate mortgages are available, lend-
Interest Act
ers have expressed some concerns about their legality with respect to the Interest Act. Bill C-36 proposes to clarify the legal status of variable rates in mortgages. Because the borrower, rather than the lender, bears the risk of interest rates changing, there would be no penalty for the prepayment of a variable rate mortgage.
Index-linked mortgages are another mortgage design that could add to the flexibility of the total mortgage market. While index-linked mortgages can be useful in certain circumstances, they are not appropriate for all borrowers. While not promoting this instrument, the Government is amending the Interest Act to permit their development if market forces dictate.
Bill C-36 proposes that the amendments apply to new mortgages on a date set by proclamation. The proposed amendments will not be applied retroactively to existing mortgages, but those mortgages will become subject to the amendments as they are renewed.
The February Budget asked lending institutions to adhere to the spirit of the proposed amendments. Many institutions have done so. We hope that they will continue to do so. Bill C-36 also contains some house-keeping amendments on judgment debts that were asked for by the provinces and will be proclaimed on a province by province basis.
At the time of the February Budget, it was announced that federal Officials would be consulting with provincial counterparts on the proposed Interest Act amendments. Consultations were also held with a committee of financial institutions and the Consumers' Association of Canada. I am pleased to report to the House that the general response to the proposed initiatives was decidedly positive. In particular, provincial consumers' affairs officials and the Consumers' Association have generally endorsed the proposals, noting that they go a long way towards improving consumer information and protection in the mortgage field.
In conclusion, Bill C-36 is a progressive piece of legislation that deals with real consumer problems caused by a lack of information and inflexibility in mortgage arrangements. The proposed amendments will improve the flexibility, vitality and functioning of the total mortgage market. The experiences of home owners during the past few years suggest that this legislation is urgently needed. I hope that this Bill can be debated quickly and sent to committee. The positive response that the proposed amendments have received from all interested parties would indicate widespread public support for Bill C-36. I trust the House will approve the Bill before the end of this current session.

Mr. Speaker, we have just heard a speech by the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren) who knows absolutely, completely and totally nothing about the mortgage industry other than what he has been told by his friends is the big trust companies, the big insurance companies and the big banks. It reminds me of the fact that he has now set up a task force which is examining the powers of the big insurance companies, the big banks and the

June 7, 1984
Interest Act
big financial lenders. He does not want to consult with the public. He gets this information from the foxes and then designs a henhouse for the foxes. The people of the country will be hurt dramatically by this legislation.
May I point out, Sir, that Section 10 of the Interest Act provides that no mortgage held by an individual can be held for longer than five years and the individual can escape his obligations under the debt instrument upon payment of three months' interest by way of bonus. This particular Bill creates a situation that is absolutely disastrous to a personal borrower who is borrowing on a term that is in excess of five years.
In the Minister's press release he gives the illustration of a mortgage of $50,000 with an interest rate of 12 per cent amortized over 25 years. In the press release he has indicated that the interest rate has presumably dropped to 9 per cent and that the term of this particular mortgage has two years yet to go. He shows that the penalty to discharge that $50,000 mortgage would be $2,538.23. Three months' interest by way of bonus would be $1,500. That is his illustration.
I asked the Department of Finance to give me the true figures with respect to someone who was unfortunate enough to sign up for a mortgage at an interest rate of 18 per cent back in the days of the Government's high interest rates which are returning again. I asked what would happen if that unfortunate person wanted to pay off his mortgage because interest rates had dropped to 13 per cent. I suggest to you, Sir, that on a two-year term rather than a three-year term or a five-year term, the penalty would be excruciatingly higher than three months' interest by way of bonus; substantially higher than six months' interest by way of bonus; probably higher than one year's interest by way of bonus. This is the kind of help that the Government wants to give to home owners. Government Members ought to be ashamed of themselves. The Minister ought to be ashamed of himself. I do not know how he can come to the House and even suggest that this Bill is designed to help home owners.
Let us take a look at the Interest Act. From my preliminary investigation I have found that we have had an Interest Act dating back to at least 1840 which has contained virtually the same terms and conditions. This Bill is in almost exactly the same form as that Act. I would suggest that it is probably in the same form as that which has been in existence since July 1, 1880. The present Interest Act is at least 100 years old and is probably much older than that.
The concepts contained within the current legislation are concepts regarding dealings between parties, lenders and borrowers, on mortgages for real estate, concepts that are a part of the common law of the country. Those concepts are well understood by people throughout the country. They are not concepts that are new. They do not involve the horrendous nonsense of the present value of future payments of money. I do not know how anyone could explain to Aunt Mamie, who may be lending money on a mortgage, the present value of future payments when she is forced to discharge the mortgage
in accordance with regulations yet unpublished, yet unthought of and yet undetermined.
It is true that a vast amount of the money in mortgages on real property or real estate in the country is money that has been put up under the auspices of financial intermediaries like the trust companies, the banks, the credit unions and the insurance companies. However, I would suggest that when dealing with the numbers of mortgage documents that exist, not necessarily in total dollar amounts, private mortgages and small trust mortgages represent more mortgage documents than the number of mortgage documents held by the large financial intermediaries. The law that is before us is a law of general application. It is a law that requires the concept that the lender is in business to lend money on mortgages for real estate not only today but 100 years from now. Aunt Mamie will be dead and buried and her estate will be long wound up by that time.
This country is a vast one. It is not made up of only Etobicoke North and Mississauga South. It is a country of small towns right across the land in which retired people, small groups of people and private merchants lend money to finance their neighbours' properties. We cannot change dramatically the terms under which interest is calculated and under which the bargain is struck without some long-term public input and without some real investigation. Such changes require a full debate and full consideration by the House.
This Bill is a bad Bill because it has been scrutinized only by the big banks, the big trust companies, the big insurance companies and the big credit unions. It has not had the scrutiny of the small town lawyers, the small town credit unions, the small finance companies, the local merchants and the people who put up money and make the country grow in the small towns and villages right across Canada. This Bill will make it virtually impossible for those people to understand the kinds of privileges that Parliament would like to see given to those who lend money on the security of real estate.
If, for example, this Bill indicated that if there were three years to go on the term of a mortgage, the bonus would be six months' interest and if there were less than three years to go on the term of a mortgage, it would be three months' interest, we could understand that and we could live with that. Even Aunt Mamie and her lawyer could understand that. However, the present value of futures in a money market somehow determined somewhere by regulations here in the ivory towers of Ottawa and presumably on the top floor of Place Bell tower is the kind of nonsense that has been spewed out by the Government for the last four and a half years and the reason why the people of the country will toss it right out.
Let us deal with the question of lending money on real estate. Somewhere along the line the Government quietly snuck in a change. The Interest Act spoke of lending money on the security of real estate. There is a great deal of difference between what is real estate and what is real property. They snuck it in with that change. Therefore, if the mortgage is a first mortgage against the title to real property, presumably the Interest Act applies. If the mortgage is a mortgage on
June 7, 1984

personalty or the equity in real property, or a mortgage against a mortgage, or a loan against a mortgage, or a loan against a mortgage on real property, it is a loan on personalty secured against real estate and the Bill will not apply. No longer will there be any protection against the hideous contracts that might be forced on the general public by the foxes that the Minister seems to support.
The Minister says that the Bill is to protect and help people. How did people get in trouble in the first place? I would refer the House to a document produced by Arthur Andersen and Company for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation respecting the objectives and overview of mortgage rate insurance. That was another disaster which the House dealt with yesterday. We will speak again on that when the Bill goes to committee. The document reads:
Two characteristics of a mortgage are: (i) the length of the period upon which the monthly payments are based; and (ii) the period during which the mortgage interest rate is fixed. When mortgages were initially introduced, and for a long period thereafter, the interest rate on the loan was fixed over the life of the mortgage. The borrower was secure in that his monthly payments were known and fixed during the entire period. The lender had either been able to borrow funds for a period that matched the life of the mortgage or was fairly certain that any changes in funding costs would be nominal. In essence, as long as interest rates remained relatively constant, lenders were prepared to offer fixed rates for the life of the mortgage.
When was that? Arthur Andersen says that it was prior to the 1970s. It was only in the 1970s that it became difficult under the present Interest Act to get a mortgage that extended beyond five years. Why? Because the governments of the day operated the country so that interest rates were relatively level. There were no massive gyrations in interest rates. The country was managed sensibly, honestly and carefully.
We are now told that that condition cannot return. Somehow we will never be able to get to a point where lenders will lend for 10 years, 20 years or 25 years as they once did. We will have to put up with variable rate mortgages, or indexed mortgages or mortgages that somehow run for short periods of time.
This country does not need to put up with that kind of mismanagement. This country should have an election soon to allow Canadians to get a set of managers who will manage the country so that interest rates will not go the way interest rates have gone during the past decade.
What is the concern? It is that because financial intermediaries want to finance with short-term money. They want to protect themselves when they lend long term, they want to ensure that they can have matching in terms of their receipt of deposits and in terms of their payment out of interest to depositors. Those people want matching and they could have matching if we had a sense of stability in the country. But rather than attempt to create a sense of stability, we had yesterday a Bill to ensure high interest rates, and today a Bill to ensure that those who borrow from mortgage companies will pay, if they want to get out of their contract, the present value of future money. This is again to ensure high interest rates and
Interest Act
to insure against the effect of instability. There is no need for that.
We are faced with what has often been referred to as Hardin's Law. It says that once there is a bad law, to correct the effects of that law, three more laws must be passed to correct that situation.
Which are equally as bad.

As my friend says "equally as bad". Of course, it implies that we must have three times three more laws, nine bad laws to cover the three bad laws which were passed to clean up the first bad law.
Let us go back to basic principles. The Interest Act has been with us for well over 100 years. It represents the basic contract that has proven itself to be a sound contract on which those who lend money and those who borrow money know where they stand. Section 10 of the Interest Act is designed to prevent lenders from tying up borrowers for longer than five years. In other words, it would give borrowers an out at the end of five years upon three months' interest to pay off the lender's claim. There has been no problem with that. That did not prevent long-term loans. But it did prevent someone gouging, harming or injuring a borrower. It was and is a form of consumer protection which we understand, know, are used. There is no need for any change in that condition.
This Bill is before us today because of the situation which developed as a result of the Government's high interest rate policy and its national energy policy which attempted to Canadianize every oil company in the world. The lack of confidence which this Government has inspired throughout the world in our economy, through the NEP and through the crude application by the Government of the Foreign Investment Review Act caused the need to keep interest rates in Canada about 6 per cent higher than those in the United States, from August 1981 to June 1982.
We are now faced with the same type of problem. We are faced with a falling dollar. Because Canada is deemed not to be a sound risk and in order to ensure that people will lend to Canada, more interest has to be paid in Canada than anywhere else to get money into Canada. That was the condition then which led people to talk about finding some way of allowing borrowers to get off the hook on mortgages.
The problem of 18 per cent and 20 per cent mortgages when interest rates fall to 12 per cent and 13 per cent arises from the fall-out of the National Energy Program, the Budget of November, 1981, of FIRA and the inept management of the economy that led to the fleeing of capital from the country. That condition can and will be changed, but to change the basic lending laws because of a government is the wrong thing to do; we must change the government.
Throughout late 1982 and 1983 people were forced to take mortgages at 18 per cent and 20 per cent. They then found they could not sell their homes with these kinds of mortgages,

June 7, 1984
Interest Act
particularly when mortgage money was available at 12 per cent to 14 per cent, so they wanted to pay off these high mortgages and refinance at a lower rate. The mortgage company had borrowed the money at the higher rate, but they said: "If you will pay our costs, we will let you off." All this Bill does is to try and institutionalize that condition; it does nothing for anyone. The penalties authorized in this Bill are so horrendous that it makes the three months' or six months' interest penalty these people would probably have to pay look pretty cheap. What is offered here is ridiculously expensive and very hard on people.
It was not as if borrowers did not know what they signed for; they knew they were tied to their mortgage contract for five years. It was the penalties they had to pay to get out of their contract that created the problem the Government is trying to react to. But it is not reacting to the problem, it is only institutionalizing a settlement which many companies made, not a very fair settlement as far as their borrowers were concerned. Our view is that there should have been a broadening of Section 10 of the Interest Act to cover more people, and make sure that the existing three months' penalty applied in more situations.
Representations were made by some of the leading companies which are now the friends of the Minister. They suggested that borrowers at 18 per cent to 20 per cent could always get out of the mortgage, even though it was a closed mortgage, with a three months' interest penalty. "That is our policy," is what some officials of Canada Trust said. But rather than go after the trust companies and the banks, rather than put the heat on, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) could easily have done, and force them to comply with what they said they would do, the Government let the large institutions get away with those misrepresentations. Rather than insist that the companies comply with the representations they made and solve the problem, the Government has come in with this statute which is really designed to make sure that the large institutions can somehow reap their pound of flesh.
Forever.

They will never be stuck again. That is a poor response to the problem.
I now want to deal with the portions of the Bill which attempt to deal with disclosure. In my province of Ontario, some 15 years ago we passed a Mortgage Brokers Arrangements Act and made the provision that mortgage brokers, lenders, had to make full and proper disclosure to the borrower. They had to be licensed, and if there were fees involved there was to be full disclosure. The disclosure form sets out the amount of money owing on the mortgage at maturity. I am told that is now the case in most provinces. Then, all of a sudden, the Ministry of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in Ottawa finds disclosure to be an important constituent matter. Well, it has always been an important constituent matter. The existing Act requires disclosure of the interest rate; it requires that the mortgage be calculated half yearly, not in advance, and there is all sorts of case law which indicates what that
means. Indeed, the lenders have published tables which indicate how much principal and interest are included in a blended payment over a period of time, calculations going to the tenth decimal point. This matter of disclosure has been covered for a long time, and it is not necessary that we in this House legislate that kind of disclosure. It is already available and working well in the provinces.
What are we going to do, ask everyone who lends money on mortgages to fill out not only the provincial forms but federal forms as well? What kind of bureaucracy are we trying to create? There is absolutely no need for the disclosure provisions proposed by the Minister in the material sent out to Members of Parliament and members of the press. Indeed, the proposals set out are poor in comparison to the existing provisions in the Province of Ontario. Therefore, why create additional paper work? You must remember that when a lender has to comply with more and more red tape, he must be paid for doing so. In other words, all his costs are paid for by borrowers, not by the Government. The money does not come from the Minister's generosity, it comes out of the pockets of borrowers. To add unnecessary red tape to the lending of money implies greater payments for the borrowers of money. There is no justification whatsoever for these provisions in the Bill.
I spoke earlier about the future value of present money being the concept on which the discharge of a mortgage prior to its maturity would be worked out. I suggest that Clause 11.2(1) (a) is unconstitutional because it affects property and civil rights by implying that by regulation the Government is somehow allowed to reduce the principal amount of money on a mortgage. That is interesting. Aunt Mamie has lent you money on a mortgage. All of sudden, by regulation passed pursuant to the discharge of the mortgage, the regulation can provide that the principal money you owe can be reduced by regulation. I am afraid that will certainly be brought before the Supreme Court of Canada and will certainly be thrown out.
While the Government has power to deal with interest rates, it has no power to deal with the principal amount owing on a mortgage. The Interest Act, the Mortgages Act and all of the other statutes do provide that no interest may be chargeable or that interest may be reduced to 5 per cent under certain conditions. But nowhere in statute law has the federal Government the power to indicate that the principal amount of the debt may be reduced. On that basis this proposal should be referred by the law officers of the Crown to the courts before it is passed by the House.
This Bill essentially guts the entire Interest Act which has been in effect since at least 1880. The last Act my researchers and I looked at was 1840. It was not quite the same but very similar. This Bill eliminates and changes Sections 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 of the present Interest Act. It also dramatically changes an anachronism which has been there for a long time dealing with interest charged on judgments in western Canada.
June 7, 1984

That shows how old this statute is. It has special provisions for the charging of interest on judgments in western Canada. They have been there since 1880. The Act has never been changed. Western Canada has since developed into provinces. It is a dramatic change in the statute.
Colonies.

My friend from Crowfoot says colonies. It was a colonial piece of legislation. This Bill changes that. With reference to those provinces the Interest Act will be changed. That is probably good.
I am essentially saying that this Bill abolishes the provisions with respect to the calculation of interest on mortgages. That statute is now part of the common law of Canada. It is a statute which lawyers and people generally in the country understand. It has no reference to regulations made by Orders in Council. The statute is clear, readable, understandable and interpreted by courts. In place of that statute is being put a whole new raft of social engineering. The Government says it has consulted the banks, trust companies and so on. However, it must consult the House of Commons, the people of the country, before it makes massive changes to the common law of the country.
This Bill should not be passed in a hurry. It should be thoroughly understood by every Member of Parliament. The proposed regulations ought to be tabled in the House. The calculation system which is proposed with respect to the early discharge of a mortgage ought to be clearly understood. It should be simple and capable of being understood by the simplest country lawyer, myself for instance. I see the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) here. It should be capable of being understood by him too. We have before us a measure which changes the system; that vitally affects the lending of money on real estate and how the interest is to be charged. We should not pass this Bill. This Bill is poorly thought out. It does not do what it is supposed to do. It does not really solve any social problem. It imposes greater penalties on borrowers. It is not a good statute for the general application of mortgage interest in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I presume that the ostensible purpose of the provisions of this Bill is to try to overcome and obviate the difficulties experienced by many people who purchased homes in 1981, 1982 and 1983. When they got their mortgages they had to make arrangements to pay monthly interest rates of 18, 19, 20 and 21 per cent. A year later they found that interest rates had dropped by 6, 7 and 8 per cent. They were stuck. When they tried to do something to reduce the exorbitant monthly payments which they were finding extremely difficult to meet, they found that they could not get out without the payment of a penalty which they had never expected and, in fact, had never been led to believe they would have to pay when they discussed the situation with their bank or mortgage company.
We are going to oppose this Bill because we believe the Bill is overly complex. It is not clear from the Bill what the
Interest Act
Government intends. The rhetoric of the Budget emphasized that more disclosure of mortgage interest information would be made available. We believe that the major benefits of the Bill which the Government is proposing will not be to the people who were caught in the situation where they had to agree to pay exorbitant interest rates to get their mortgage. The major beneficiaries of this Bill will be the banks and mortgage companies.
The prepayment rights and penalties sections of this Bill may sound good, but it is a nothing proposal. The Government wants to allow borrowers to have the right to prepay at any time. However, the penalty for doing so would be the full amount of interest due between the day one prepays and the day that the mortgage term expires. In other words, the person who has the mortgage would pay all the interest in any case. The Government would like to see that the borrower does not have to pay for the privilege of paying all of the interest sooner, but this represents no break to the borrower. For example, if one is locked into an 18.5 per cent mortgage of $50,000 for five years and has three years until the term expires but would like to renegotiate, the prepayment penalty would be $7,855 which represents 36 months of payments at 12.5 per cent rather than 18.5 per cent.
In the period between 1981 and 1983 I, as I suspect every other Member of Parliament, was receiving calls from constituents who found themselves in a situation where they had agreed to take a mortgage at a very high interest rate but a year later the interest rate on mortgages had come down very sharply. One could not blame them for wanting to renegotiate their mortgage so they could pay the much lower interest rate. When they went to the bank they discovered that the bank was imposing new rules and procedures. They then went to their Member of Parliament. We made representations to the banks and mortgage companies but were unsuccessful. We made representations to the Minister of Finance who told us that these matters could be cleared up by referring them to the appropriate Minister. He said he would look after it.
Some of us took all of those steps but with no results. Our constituents were stuck with these very high mortgage rates. Let me put on the record one illustration of what happened to one of my constituents. It is a good illustration because it is typical of what was happening right across the country. I will read a few sentences from the letter which was sent to me by this constituent explaining what happened. This occurred in 1982. This constituent says:
I took the mortgage out as of July 1st, 1982, at 183/4 per cent-
I asked (the manager) what would happen if the rate dropped considerably. He told me that I would be charged a three-month penalty, that they take my mortgage payments times three, and that would be the penalty to discharge my mortgage. He told me it would cost approximately $2,200-
He also told me that 1 would be saving approximately $3,000 by doing this.
This is when the person wanted to renegotiate the mortgage because the interest rates had come down by 6 per cent or 7 per cent. This constituent went to her lawyer because she was not certain that she understood everything. Her lawyer spoke

June 7, 1984
Interest Act
to the branch manager who confirmed the situation, but when they tried to pay the three-month penalty so they could get a new mortgage at the much lower rate, they were suddenly told by the local branch manager that the instruction had come from the head office that the penalty would be almost $5,000. The poor bank could not afford to do it any cheaper.
In order to make certain that I had a clear understanding of what had happened, I got in touch with the local branch manager. He confirmed what my constituent had told me. I then wrote to the head of the Toronto-Dominion Bank and outlined the situation to him. I asked him to explain why this had happened. I suggested that the bank could really show some consideration for this constituent.
Eventually, I received a reply from the Vice-President of the Toronto-Dominion Bank, William Clarkson. I will read part of his letter into the record:
The mortgage which Mr. and Mrs. Silvari contracted for in May 1982 is a standard C.M.H.C. mortgage which, in effect, provides for no prepayment other than 10 per cent of the original amount of the mortgage on each anniversary date, for the first three year term. After three years has elapsed, the mortgagor has the privilege of payment paying the full amount of the loan on payment of an amount equal to three months' interest at the contract rate.
Later he said:
Because of the large number of mortgage customers involved, it is quite simply beyond our resources to cushion the impact of high interest rates for our borrowers, nor could we do it selectively as it would be impossible to set criteria that would be fair and equitable to all. We regret that, because of the circumstances outlined, we are unable at this time to modify the amount of the payment required to renegotiate the terms of the Silvaris' mortgage.
The banks are all the same. They made over $1 billion in profits last year on which they paid very little taxes because of the very generous way in which the Liberal Government of Canada treats the banks. These poor banks, which need so much assistance, are the most powerful business organizations in the country. Not only do they control the financial services but because of their interlocking directorships they control virtually all large businesses and corporations in this country. The poor banks could do nothing for my constituent or any of the other Canadians who were caught in this very tough squeeze.
I took the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) at his word when I and other Members on this side of the House, both NDP and Conservative, appealed to him publicly in the House to do something. We were assured by the Minister that he would and could do something about it. He inferred that in some way we had not done our jobs as we should have. I am sure that Liberal Members of Parliament were getting similar complaints from their constituents and were taking them up with the Minister of Finance not publicly but privately. I am sure they were getting the same kind of assurances.
I wrote to the Minister of Finance and took him at his word that these matters could be straightened out so that those who were caught in this squeeze could get better treatment and a small modicum of justice. I sent the Minister the particulars of the case which I have just illustrated, including the correspondence from my constituent and the replies I got from the Toronto-Dominion Bank. What did I get from the Minister of
Finance? He explained that the banks, of course, had loaned people money for their mortgages and that they had reinvested the interest they received in fixed-term investments and were therefore stuck. In his letter to me, his offer of assistance to these people who were really caught in this unconsionable squeeze was as follows:
In certain cases, if a homeowner is facing financial hardship as a result of renewing his or her mortgage at high interest rates, the federal government will grant up to $3,000 under the Canada Mortgage Renewal Plan. This plan falls within the jurisdiction of the Honourable Minister responsible for Housing. If you believe that your constituents might be able to benefit from the Canada Mortgage Renewal Plan, may I suggest that they contact the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation-
That, of course, was of no help to my constituents. This Bill drops the present requirement on prepayment of a mortgage of five years or longer of paying a penalty of up to three months' interest. Whom does that benefit, Mr. Speaker? It does not benefit the borrower; it benefits the banks and the mortgage companies who lend the money. Section 10 of the Interest Act provides that after five years mortgages can be repaid with an interest penalty of three months. This provision is now to be eliminated, presumably so that the long-term mortgage market can be revived. I do not believe we will ever see a long-term mortgage market again. The days are gone when one could get a mortgage for 20 or 25 years at a rate which would not change over that period.
This is an interesting proposal if only because both Opposition Parties, and I am sure privately some back-bench Liberal Members of Parliament, have been calling for the standardization of the three-month interest penalty. This change is being introduced "to ensure that mortgage funds are available to meet the demand".
The Government brought forward Bill C-36 with the suggestion that it will help people buy a home and take out a mortgage in order to finance the purchase of that home. This Bill helps not the person who is buying a house, who arranges to pay for the house by getting a mortgage from a bank or a trust company; if it helps anybody, this Bill helps precisely the institutions which have used the high and fluctuating interest rates on mortgages we have had in recent years as well to gouge the person who arranges a mortgage.
Because this Bill benefits those who have instead of those who have not, because this Bill benefits the lender rather than the borrower, because it is doing exactly the reverse of what it should be doing, we intend to oppose it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) for debate.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-36 which is before the House to amend the Interest Act has much broader ramifications than might have been indicated by the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren) when he was presenting the Bill to the House of Commons.
Interest rates are at the heart of the housing problem both in terms of the home owner because of the problems of
June 7, 1984

mortgage interest rates which face a home owner, and the problems of providing an adequate supply of housing since construction of housing units is affected by interest rates, these are both aspects of the equation.
Let me review very briefly the history of mortgage rates in Canada. We went through a long period, 1951 to 1972, when interest rates were below double-digit figures; that is, they were below 10 per cent. On one or two occasions, however, mortgage interest rates did rise to 10 per cent during that time. But since 1972, almost 13 years, Canadians have been faced with double-digit mortgage interest rates and people seeking to finance a home have been forced to pay 10 per cent or more. Unfortunately, at certain periods within that time frame Canadians have paid interest rates like 21.46 per cent and 19.22 per cent, the latter in 1982. Now in April, May and June, 1984 Canadians are facing mortgage interest rates rising to 14.25 per cent. There is no indication that those rates will not rise over the next six months. Hopefully they will not rise to the high which occurred in September, 1981 of 21.46 per cent.
High mortgage interest rates are the problem, Mr. Speaker. How do they affect Canadians? They affect them in very specific terms. The cost of a $90,000 mortgage at 18 per cent is $1,346 a month. Contrast that with a more reasonable mortgage interest rate of 10 per cent. On that same $90,000 mortgage, the payment would be $847 a month. This means almost $500 a month more to the person who happens to be unfortunate enough to face a mortgage rate of 18 per cent when he should be entitled to a mortgage rate more in the area of 10 per cent.
Let us now look at a mortgage of $50,000. At 18 per cent the monthly payment would be $747. That same $50,000 mortgage at 10 per cent costs $476 a month. A person pays $271 a month more at 18 per cent. Now, whether you enjoy a home carrying a $70,000 mortgage or a home carrying a $50,000 mortgage, in proportionate terms you have the same problem. A mortgage payment on a $90,000 mortgage is increased by $500 at 18 per cent and on a mortgage of $50,000 is increased by $271 at 18 per cent. You can see, Mr. Speaker, how that difference in mortgage payments at the higher level dramatically affects the budget of a Canadian family. How many Canadians are in that position? In 1983 there were approximately 5.3 million home owners in Canada, the great majority of whom had mortgages on their homes. We are talking about a tremendous number of people who are affected by this problem of mortgage rates.
It is with those people in mind that we have to approach a Bill like, Bill C-36 and examine it in that context. I want to direct my remarks in response to the Minister. The Minister mentioned as a highlight of this Bill the matter of full disclosure. That is a deception of serious proportions. Bill C-36 with respect to disclosure of mortgage provisions adds nothing to the existing law that will benefit any Canadian. In 1966 the Province of Nova Scotia enacted the first Consumer Protection Act in Canada. Other provinces followed very quickly thereafter. The thrust of those provisions in legislation like the
Interest Act
Consumer Protection Act was to require mortgagees and other lenders to disclose in exact terms the rate of interest charged and other conditions of the loan. Canadians have enjoyed the advantage of that kind of protective legislation for almost 20 years. When the Minister boasts that he is introducing in the House of Commons legislative provisions intended to protect Canadians in terms of the conditions of mortgage loans, he and his Government add nothing to the protection already provided to them under provincial legislation.
The Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) pointed out that the Interest Act is ancient legislation. While consumer protection legislation does not have the same antiquity, it has certainly been in force for a sufficient length of time to have established that in consumer loan transactions, including mortgage transactions, lenders are at present required to disclose in a very careful way the terms and conditions of mortgages.
I want to point out the downside of the new provisions. There may even be a disadvantage to the additional provisions which the Government proposes in Bill C-36. As has already been pointed out by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South, there is a price for these disclosure provisions and that price is paid by consumers. It can be set up any way, but the ultimate cost of all goods and services provided in Canada are paid for by Canadian consumers. Although it may appear on the surface that the lender is bearing some of the costs of the disclosure provisions, we can rest assured that those costs will be paid in the long run by consumers.
If the Minister's additional protective provisions add to the cost of the mortgage transaction by increasing the paperwork and increasing administrative services required to conform to the new law, then it will be an additional cost burden which will eventually be paid for by consumers. I caution the Minister to review that aspect of Bill C-36 and ensure that, in carrying out the pretence of additional protections and benefits for Canadian consumers in the mortgage market, the Government is not simply adding to the costs which consumers eventually will have to bear.
A second remark made by the Minister in his introductory comments was that Bill C-36 was urgently needed. I do not think anyone would argue about the seriousness of the mortgage problem in Canada in respect of Canadian home owners and those seeking to acquire homes. However, I want to point out that the Minister and his colleagues in government have a very strange attitude toward the urgency. On December 8, 1983, in the Speech from the Throne, the Government proposed a package of mortgage protection for Canadians. Again in the Budget Speech of February 15, 1984 reference was made to a package of protection for Canadian home owners faced with mortgage problems. It is only now in June, 1984 that we have come to deal with the legislation intended to implement this promise made to Canadians in December, 1983.
4432

June 7, 1984
Interest Act
I ask the Minister how he views this as responding to an urgent need. It took over six months to fulfil the promise made in the Speech from the Throne in December, 1983. If the Government did not know what kind of legislation it contemplated in its protective package, why did it make that promise in the Speech from the Throne? Why did it not simply say that it would consider some protective measures and bring them forward at a later date? Instead, Canadians were led to believe that they would receive immediate protection. I remind Government Members that many Canadians who are faced with mortgage renewals would look very carefully at promises of assistance and watch longingly and with a great deal of concern for these legislative remedies to be presented to Parliament. I am sure those Canadians will not be very pleased with the Government's version of immediate action in response to what it admits is an urgent situation.
Also in his remarks the Minister mentioned an industrial task force to deal with mortgage interest rates and solutions to the problems created by the Interest Act. While I agree with consultation between government and those involved in the industry, this decision on the matter of mortgage interest rates and what is a fair price for cancelling a mortgage transaction is a decision which has to be made by the Government of Canada in the interests of all Canadians. It may well be important to consult with loan companies or companies engaged in the mortgage business, but the Government has to take into account the welfare of Canadians in making that decision. It cannot rely upon representations and discussions with institutions in the mortgage industry which have, after all, a vested interest. They must put forward the interests of their own clientele and investors.
However, I remind Government Members that housing is one of the most important needs of Canadians. The availability of mortgage funds to provide housing is part and parcel of the response to that need. The Government cannot simply come up with a formula which is satisfactory to lenders and put it forward as the proper solution to the problem. The Government must consider what Canadians need in the way of housing and in the way of assistance to provide themselves with adequate housing, and make the decision on that basis. While consultation with industry is important, it does not forgive the Government for making a decision which may be consistent with the advice it receives from those in industry but is not consistent with the welfare of Canadians who are seeking to maintain their homes or those who are seeking to acquire homes. That is the test which must be applied to this legislation. Does it help Canadians in maintaining their homes? Does it assist Canadians who are seeking to acquire homes?
In that respect one must conclude that the legislation fails. Why does it fail? It fails because it introduces a complex formula or method of dealing with a very simple problem- what is the proper and fair way to discharge an existing mortgage when the debtor under the mortgage has to make the difficult decision that he or she can no longer afford to carry the mortgage and must cancel it? They are either forced to sell
their homes or to move to another place and acquire new homes.
The Hon. Member for Mississauga South has very graphically and clearly discussed this aspect of the problem. However, I want to make the plea on my own behalf that the proper method to deal with the problem of the cancellation of mortgages is a simple formula, one which is fair to the lender and fair to the mortgagor but which at the same time reflects the vital need of all Canadians for adequate housing. If there are to be errors made in the construction of that simple formula, then they have to be made on the side of home owners.
Along with the Hon. Member for Mississauga South, I propose that there be a simple penalty based upon monthly interest payments. Whatever may be selected, from one month to six months, it should be the basis for the amount charged when a mortgage debtor seeks to cancel a mortgage transaction. A fair level would be three months; that is to say, a mortgage debtor who seeks to cancel a mortgage would pay a three months' penalty. It is difficult to know whether that figure should be six or one, but three appears to be reasonable. If there is going to be any error, it should be on the side of the home owner who has no method of recovery for losses as opposed to the mortgage lender who has other methods to recoup any losses that may be suffered.
If that sounds too arbitrary and unfair, let me explain it. With mortgage penalties for cancellation of mortgage transactions, as in all other transactions involving consumers, what we have to attempt to achieve through legislation is a balance of rights. We have to balance the rights between lenders and borrowers in a fair way. As I have said, if there are going to be errors made, they should be made in favour of the borrowers rather than lenders, because in the long run that is in the interest of all Canadians. In seeking to balance those rights, the Government has the obligation to make the decision. It cannot slough off that legislation obligation on a committee composed of government, consumer and industrial representatives. It is a decision that has to be made by the Government.
It is clear in Bill C-36 that the Government has avoided taking its responsibility. In response to the consultations it has held, the Government has come up with a method that is simply a failure to make a decision. The method chosen by the Government, alleged to be flexible, is simply to enact regulations from time to time to set up the formula. That is not making a decision: it is avoiding a decision.
It is very difficult to take the legislation as a serious attempt to resolve the problems that exist under the current Interest Act with respect to the cancellation of mortgage transactions. The Government knows there is a problem. As Members have said time and time again, the problem comes up as mortgage interest rates escalate. The Government must realize that some action has to be taken. Its answer was to present a Bill which does not provide a solution. That does not provide an answer; it
June 7, 1984

merely finesses the whole problem to regulations that will be made at some future time.
Even though the Government proposed these legislative enactments seven months ago, the regulations are not available. Nobody knows what the regulations will be. Canadians are being asked to accept a pig in a poke, legislation that does not answer the question or respond to the needs. Everyone will have to wait for future developments to find out whether the effects of the legislation are fair or adverse. That is not acceptable. It is appropriate that Members of this House of Commons underline the failure of the Government to respond to this evident need. We should underline the failure of the Government to come up with a solution that Canadians can examine and then determine for themselves whether it meets the test of balancing rights between mortgage lenders and mortgage debtors. The Government is copping out, failing to make a decision. It leaves Canadians in the dark as to what the attitude is with respect to the vital matter of mortgages, mortgage interest rates and the cancellation of mortgage transactions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are there questions or comments?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has practised law both in Ontario and in Nova Scotia. Can he explain the type of disclosure required in the Province of Nova Scotia with respect to those who lend money on mortgages, mortgage brokers and so on? What type of disclosure is required in Nova Scotia? In his speech, the Hon. Member mentioned that the disclosure provisions are not required, that provinces have disclosure provisions and this is a duplication of a kind of disclosure already required.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South has struck a very interesting chord in his question, particularly as it relates to the Provinces of Nova Scotia and Ontario. As I indicated, Nova Scotia was the first province in Canada to enact consumer protection legislation. That occurred in 1966 when the legislature of the Province of Nova Scotia enacted the Consumer Protection Act. It should be admitted that the provisions of that Consumer Protection Act were based on a report that emanated from the Government of the Province of Ontario, a Progressive Conservative Government that had examined the problem concerning consumers in relation to loan transactions, particularly mortgage transactions. It recommended that certain disclosure requirements be enforced through law.
Nova Scotia acted upon that kind of advice and that of other legislative committees that had studied the matter and formulated the Consumer Protection Act. That Act has been in force since 1966, with amendments intended and designed to meet needs as they arose over that period of time.
To deal directly with the Hon. Member's question, the Consumer Protection Act of Nova Scotia, and I am certain there is similar legislation in every other province, requires that a lender advise the borrower of the exact interest rate that will be enforced throughout the life of a loan, and that includes
Interest Act
a mortgage loan, so that the borrower knows exactly the rate of interest, the basis for calculating that interest and the amount. The concern of most consumers and most mortgage borrowers is the amount they will have to pay on a monthly basis. The consumer protection provisions require full and proper disclosure of the exact amount that will have to be paid throughout the life of a loan. In addition, there is a requirement that the mortgage borrower be advised of the rate of interest in exactitude. That means the ancillary provisions and whether it is calculated annually, semi-annually, cumulatively and so on. All of that information must be given not only to mortgage borrowers but to all borrowers of funds in consumer situations.
In addition, there are other specific requirements that relate to all loan transactions. The borrower must be informed of the place of business of the lender and other vital statistics. The matter is completely covered. To the extent that it is not covered, I am sure simple amendments to provincial legislation would cover any other areas that might give rise to problems.

Mr. Speaker, I commend the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) for a very interesting and excellent address. He is not only highly trained but is a highly experienced barrister.
I would like to get his view on a matter. When interest rates were at their highest, I had a number of cases concerning my constituents. One problem in particular comes to mind at this time. A family suddenly came into sufficient money to pay off their mortgage. If I recall correctly, the interest rate was 18 per cent. They went to the trust company which held the mortgage and reminded it of its promise that they could pay off the mortgage with a two-month penalty. The trust company said that could not be done, that there would be a two-year penalty because the money had been invested in a long-term investment. Therefore, the family was told they had to pay a two-year penalty in order to get out of the mortgage.
I thought that was outrageous. I referred the matter to the Minister of Finance because he had indicated in the House that he wanted these kinds of cases brought to his attention. I brought it to his attention and he sent me a letter containing a list of all the trust companies and telling me to write to them myself. That was not very helpful.
I did write to the mortgage companies and they were able to do very little for my constituent. They continued to say that they had invested in long-term investments. I reminded the mortgage companies that many of their investments were short-term investments and perhaps the majority of them were short-term investments. I would like to hear the comment of the Hon. Member for Halifax West regarding what a reasonable penalty would be when a family is able to pay off its mortgage. What would be fair to both the mortgagor and the mortgagee?

Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), has described the classic case and

June 7, 1984
Interest Act
asked the classic question. I know that he believes as I do that a lender should be entitled to fair compensation for the cancellation of a transaction, but he should not be entitled to a windfall profit arising from the good fortune-or the misfortune-of the borrower. When answering that question in terms of the law that we enact, we must try to achieve a balance between those two rights.
I can best answer the question of the Hon. Member for Bow River by going back a bit in time to see what the developments in the mortgage market in Canada have been in relation to the Interest Act that is now before us and in relation to Section 10 of that Act. For many decades, the classic mortgage system in Canada was that a mortgage was held for a 25-year term. In more recent times that was reduced to a five-year term after which time the mortgage interest rate was renewed. That term has now been reduced to as little as one year.
The reason I mention this bit of history is that for many years the mortgage provision in the Interest Act was that if a mortgage ran for more than five years-and most mortgages ran for at least 20 years-that mortgage could be paid off after a five-year term with a payment equal to three months' interest. I believe I am correct about that but the Hon. Member for Mississauga South can correct me if I am not. In other words, the so-called penalty was based on the monthly interest rate in relation to that mortgage. However, there was no provision for mortgages with terms of less than five years. That is to say, such a borrower was left to the provisions of the mortgage or to the good offices of the lender. That is the situation in which the constituents of the Hon. Member found themselves. There was no clear provision in law with respect to their rights when paying off the mortgage.
In those circumstances, many mortgage lenders claim that they have taken money from their investors and promised to pay them a rate of interest over a long period of time, like five years, and they then take the attitude that the only fair thing is for them to receive all of the revenues that they would have received had the borrower kept the money he had borrowed for that entire period of time. Of course, that is an extreme position and it is a ridiculous one. Unfortunately, that was the position taken by many of Canada's foremost lenders, including the banks and large mortgage companies. That is why we as legislators must step into that situation and make our judgment with respect to what is fair. The thrust of my position is that the Government should make that judgment. Such penalties should be based upon a monthly interest payment and I think the penalty should be no more than three months' interest.

Mr. Speaker, when speaking today on Bill C-36, the amendments to the Interest Act, I will go backwards. I shall begin with the last provisions in the Bill which is before us, being Clauses 4 and 5 which deal with the interest payable on judgment debts.
I am pleased to see that the amendment regarding judgment debts is before us today. In effect, what it does is remove an anachronism that has existed since 1880 or even longer. At that time the Provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan did not exist but were contained within the Northwest Territories. Ever since Confederation the eastern provinces had within their legislative authority the ability to specify the interest payable on judgment debts. It makes no sense to have one law affecting eastern Canada and a different law affecting western Canada.
I would hope that the western provinces and the western territories which, as a result of the passage of this Bill, will have the authority to stipulate in their own legislation the interest payable on judgment debts will take upon themselves the responsibility to do so as soon as possible. However, when doing so I would hope that they would keep in mind that as much as possible interest payable on judgment debts should be uniform across Canada.
Although I agree that it should be within the authority of the province or territory to set these rates, it does not make much sense if the rate is 5 per cent in one province, 7.5 per cent in another province and 10 per cent in another province. I think that the provinces and territories should get together and try to come up with a uniform rate if that is at all possible. As well, when changes are made the provinces should act in concert to keep those rates reasonably uniform across Canada.
Again working from the back of the Bill forward, the next prime issue contained therein is that dealing with disclosure. This deals with what, by law, should be disclosed within a mortgage document. Items dealing with disclosure were contained in Section 6 of the old Act. This is certainly not a new concept.
Today we heard that many provinces go much further than the federal Parliament when requiring disclosure of certain terms and conditions with respect to mortgages. The point has been made that most mortgage lenders are already obliged to comply with the provincial requirements and that some difficulty and additional expense might be imposed upon them by making it necessary at the same time for them to comply with federal legislation. Although those additional expenses would be minor, I would imagine that the difficulties could be worked out so the lenders could easily comply with both provincial and federal disclosure requirements.
In reading through the proposed changes to Section 6 of the Act which are contained in Clause 2 of the Bill before us, what strikes me is some of the new things that will have to be disclosed. In 1880, the year the present Act was passed by the Parliament of the day, if someone had suggested that at some point in the future of Canada we would be thinking about mortgages with terms and conditions dealing with changes in principle because of inflation, the legislators of that day would not have had the foggiest idea what he was talking about.
In those days the term of a mortgage was generally a period of 20 years or more. There was an element of stability to mortgages. The terms and conditions were reasonably simple. They were such that someone who homesteaded a farm in
June 7, 1984

Alberta or Saskatchewan, although those provinces did not exist at the time, would understand along with legal counsel in the small settlements what they were all about.
I see that it is very close to one o'clock. I might call it one o'clock, Sir, and continue this afternoon.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-ACTION BY MAYORS AND REEVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring to the attention of this House the fact that a delegation of mayors and reeves from the Fraser Valley of British Columbia is presently in Ottawa. Mayor John Agnew from Mission, Danny Griffin from Maple Ridge, Danny Sharpe from Pitt Meadows, John Jansen from Chilliwack, Paul Inkman from Harrison Hot Springs, Lloyd Foreman from Boston Bar, and Brian Appleby from Dudney-Allouette regional district are here to discuss and co-ordinate a plan of direct action to resolve catastrophically high levels of unemployment. It bears emphasizing again that in the area of Mission-Port Moody and Fraser Valley East average unemployment stood between 14 per cent and 15 per cent. However, with the shake and shingle mill shut down, the rate stands at an alarming 47 per cent to 52 per cent. If one takes into account the native population, the rate climbs to an astonishing 58 per cent.
A Fraser Valley College private study pointed out that the job situation is devastating. There could be as many as 15,000 young people in that area looking for jobs this summer. The problem of unemployment must be dealt with swiftly. I appreciate the commitment given by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts) and I now look to him to flesh out the particulars of the LEAD program and the reforestation assistance program. This is an opportunity to show that the Government can respond to Canadian citizens who are really in need. I urge all Ministers and officials who are meeting with this delegation to do their utmost to help in trying to resolve this terrible unemployment problem.

maintopic: CONSTRUCTION OF HEAVY OIL UPGRADER IN LLOYDMINSTER, SASK.
CONSTRUCTION OF HEAVY OIL UPGRADER IN LLOYDMINSTER, SASK.

maintopic: WESTERN GRAIN FREIGHT RATES-COST TO FARMERS
WESTERN GRAIN FREIGHT RATES-COST TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, western Canadian farmers are in danger of buckling under the weight of a projected 58 per cent increase in the cost of moving grain. As a result of the Liberals' Crow Bill, each western grain producer will pay, on average, between $500 and $1,500 more to move grain in the next crop year. That is an extremely heavy burden for a sector already enduring extremely trying times.
The cause for virtually the entire increase coming up in August is the cap on the amount of western grain shipments subsidized by the federal Government. Because prairie grain shipments will exceed the 31.5 million tonne cap in the current crop year, the producers will have to pay the full freight rate on more than 3 million tonnes of grain in the coming crop year, an additional $60 million in total. As well as being the cause of a dramatic freight increase, the cap is also a disincentive to improved western grain production. Surely a disincentive to food production is in no one's best interest.
It is my understanding that the Minister of Transport has directed the Special Grain Transportation Committee to review this matter. I urge the Minister to ensure, not only that the issue is studied soon, but that the opinions of groups representing western grain producers are reflected in any decision taken. The Crow Bill and other Liberal Government policies have caused financial hardship for far too many prairie farmers. I call upon the Government to put the needs of western Canada first for once, by abolishing the volume cap on subsidized prairie grain shipments.

The formula which is being used could not be based only on Statistics Canada data, because such data are not compiled on a constituency basis. We are using, therefore, a mixed formula which nevertheless takes into account local situations; it is being applied across the board to 281 ridings in Canada. Because there is no official Statistics Canada formula, we are using a statistical formula which applies to all ridings, whether Conservative, NDP or Liberal.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister. The Acting Prime Minister may be aware that an article in this morning's Globe and Mail by the immediate past chairman of the Canada Council, Mavor Moore, stated:
According to several members of the Canada Council living in various parts of the country, the Deputy Minister of Communications, Robert Rabinovitch, recently telephoned the director of the Canada Council, Timothy Porteous and instructed him that public criticism of the Government's plan in Bill C-24 by himself, or the staff or even members of the Council's board, would not be tolerated.
That squares with the testimony we heard on Tuesday from Brian Anthony, executive director of the Canadian Conference of the Arts, who said:
We have been led to believe that it would be inappropriate for any agency to risk its good standing and well-being at this moment by speaking out against Bill C-24.

speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
subsubtopic: REPORTED TELEPHONE CALL TO DIRECTOR FROM DEPUTY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Deputy Minister of Communications emphatically denies that he exerted any pressure or intimidation on the executive director of the Canada Council. He denies that. The conversation he had with the said gentleman was at the request of the Minister, with the consent of his own Minister, and consequently quite within the rules of his function.
The Canada Council will be before the committee this afternoon, at the request of the Minister, who suggested that they should appear before the committee on the discussion of Bill C-24 and these questions can be raised there.
The Government intends to respect the tradition of autonomy which exists for cultural agencies in Canada, but there is also a tradition of accountability that must be reconciled with the tradition of autonomy. These subjects are very important and will be discussed this afternoon before the committee.

Mr. Speaker, the gravity of the situation may not be clear to the Acting Prime Minister. The atmosphere of fear and intimidation of which I speak has been with us for a number of weeks. There are a number of groups which have failed to come forward because they fear the consequences for their own funding. Since it involves not merely the Canada Council but, as Brian Anthony pointed out, and he speaks for many arts organizations across the country, given the intimidation, these organizations are considering having to take "a dive" because they fear the intimidation from the Government, will the Acting Prime Minister undertake in this House to investigate other allegations which have been made with respect to cultural organizations beyond the Canada Council which had been intimidated as well?

speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I really do not know to what allegations my friend is referring. Certainly the Canada Council was not intimidated. If there are groups in Canada which feel intimidated, they will have an opportunity to express that fear. The committee is one place where they can do so.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of International Trade. As the Minister knows, armed conflict is growing in the State of Punjab in India.
